title: Unit Digit Cycles for Powers
tagline: Year 3 — The repeating pattern of last digits and how to read it for very large powers

introduction.overview: The last digit of a power depends only on the last digit of the base, and the last digits of successive powers repeat in a short cycle. Knowing the cycle for each digit lets you find the unit digit of numbers like 7^2023 without computing them. The same idea, extended to two digits, gives the last two digits of a power.
introduction.placementRelevance: Unit-digit questions are commonly asked in company aptitude rounds, usually as "the unit digit of 7^123 + 3^45" or of a product of several powers.
introduction.realWorldContext: Checksums, hashing and calendar-like cycles are built on the same repeating patterns.

learningObjectives: Know the cycle of unit digits for bases 0 to 9
Reduce the exponent by the cycle length
Handle sums and products of powers
Find the last two digits of a power
Handle tower exponents such as a^(b^c)

prerequisiteKnowledge.quickRefresher: The unit digit of a product is the unit digit of the product of the unit digits. For a sum, add the unit digits.

coreDefinitions: Cycle length (period): the number of steps after which the unit digits repeat.
Cycles: 0, 1, 5, 6 have length 1; 4 and 9 have length 2; 2, 3, 7, 8 have length 4.
Exponent reduction: the unit digit of aⁿ depends on n modulo the cycle length (use the full cycle when the remainder is 0).
conceptExplanation.theoreticalIntuition: Only the last digit is ever needed, so the base can be replaced by its last digit. Then the powers cycle, and a huge exponent is just a position in a short cycle.
conceptExplanation.visualOrMentalModel: Take the last digit of the base, recall its cycle, divide the exponent by the cycle length and use the remainder as the position (a remainder 0 means the last element of the cycle).

importantRulesAndFormulas.title: Reducing the exponent
importantRulesAndFormulas.description: Use the cycle of the last digit.

importantRulesAndFormulas.title: Sums and products
importantRulesAndFormulas.formula: Unit digit of the sum or product of the unit digits
importantRulesAndFormulas.description: Compute each term's unit digit first.

importantRulesAndFormulas.title: Towers
importantRulesAndFormulas.formula: Unit digit of a^(b^c): reduce b^c modulo the cycle length of a

mainNarrative: Take the last digit of the base. Powers of 7 end in 7, 9, 3, 1 and repeat every 4. For 7^123, 123 = 4 × 30 + 3, so the unit digit is the 3rd in the cycle: 3.
When the exponent is a multiple of the cycle length, the unit digit is the last element of the cycle. 2^100: the cycle 2, 4, 8, 6 has length 4 and 100 is a multiple of 4, so the unit digit is 6.
For sums and products, take unit digits term by term. 2^2023 ends in 8 (2023 mod 4 = 3) and 3^2024 ends in 1 (2024 mod 4 = 0), so the product ends in 8 and the sum ends in 9.
Digits 4 and 9 have a cycle of 2: the powers of 4 end in 4 if the exponent is odd and 6 if even; the powers of 9 end in 9 if odd and 1 if even.
For a tower such as 2^(3^2), compute the exponent first: 3² = 9, then 2⁹: 9 mod 4 = 1, so the unit digit is 2. For the last two digits, 7⁴ = 2401 ends in 01, so 7^(4k) ends in 01.

deepDiveAspects.title: Last two digits of powers of 7
deepDiveAspects.content: 7¹ = 07, 7² = 49, 7³ = 43, 7⁴ = 01, then it repeats every 4. So 7^100 ends in 01 and 7^101 in 07.

deepDiveAspects.title: Why factorials end in 0
deepDiveAspects.content: From 5! onward every factorial contains the factors 2 and 5, so the unit digit is 0. Only 1! to 4! (1, 2, 6, 24) matter.

solvedExamples.title: Unit digit of a power
solvedExamples.question: Find the unit digit of 7¹²³.
solvedExamples.commonTrap: Using the exponent itself instead of its remainder.

solvedExamples.title: Product of powers
solvedExamples.question: Find the unit digit of 2²⁰²³ × 3²⁰²⁴.
solvedExamples.commonTrap: Treating remainder 0 as the first element.

shortcutMethods.title: Cycle table

traditionalVsShortcut.shortcutMethod: Remember the cycles of 2, 3, 7, 8 (length 4), 4, 9 (length 2) and read the position from the exponent remainder.

rulesForApplication: Remainder 0 means the last in the cycle.
For last two digits, find a power ending in 01.

commonMistakes.whyItHappens: Reading the first element for a multiple of the cycle length.
commonMistakes.howToAvoid: Use the last element of the cycle.

commonMistakes.mistake: Forgetting that unit digit of a sum needs unit digits of terms

placementTips.eliminationTechnique: Unit digits of squares can only be 0, 1, 4, 5, 6 or 9; reject other options in square questions.
placementTips.questionSelectionAdvice: Memorise the four cycles of length 4.
placementTips.recruiterInsight: Unit-digit questions are very fast once the table is known.

easy.question: The unit digit of 7¹²³ is
easy.explanation: The cycle of 7 is 7, 9, 3, 1. 123 leaves remainder 3 on division by 4, giving 3.

easy.question: The unit digit of 2¹⁰⁰ is
easy.explanation: The cycle of 2 is 2, 4, 8, 6. 100 is a multiple of 4, so the unit digit is 6.

easy.question: The unit digit of 4¹⁰¹ is
easy.explanation: The powers of 4 end in 4 for odd exponents: 4.

intermediate.question: The unit digit of 2²⁰²³ × 3²⁰²⁴ is
intermediate.explanation: 2²⁰²³ ends in 8 and 3²⁰²⁴ ends in 1. The product ends in 8.

intermediate.question: The unit digit of 7⁴⁵ + 3⁴⁵ is
intermediate.explanation: 7⁴⁵ ends in 7 and 3⁴⁵ ends in 3 (45 leaves 1 on division by 4). 7 + 3 = 10, so the unit digit is 0.

intermediate.question: The unit digit of 1! + 2! + 3! + … + 50! is
intermediate.explanation: 5! and above end in 0. 1 + 2 + 6 + 24 = 33, so the unit digit is 3.

advanced.question: The unit digit of 7^(7^7) is
advanced.explanation: Find 7⁷ modulo 4: 7 ≡ −1, so 7⁷ ≡ −1 ≡ 3. Then 7³ ends in 3.

placementStyle.question: The last two digits of 7⁹⁹ are
placementStyle.explanation: 7⁴ ≡ 01 (mod 100). 99 = 4 × 24 + 3, so 7⁹⁹ ≡ 7³ = 343 ≡ 43. The last two digits are 43.

placementStyle.question: The unit digit of 17¹⁷ × 13¹³ × 19¹⁹ is
placementStyle.explanation: 17¹⁷ ends in 7, 13¹³ ends in 3, 19¹⁹ ends in 9. 7 × 3 = 21 → 1, then 1 × 9 = 9. The unit digit is 9.

placementStyle.question: The unit digit of 2²⁰²⁴ + 3²⁰²⁴ is
placementStyle.explanation: 2²⁰²⁴ ends in 6 and 3²⁰²⁴ ends in 1. The sum ends in 7.

selfCheckQuestions: Can I find the unit digit of 7^123?
Can I handle a product of two powers?
Can I find the last two digits of 7^100?
